title: Tryptophan Challenge Study, Cologne Investigation of the role of diet in microbiome-mediated AhR activation and associated inflammatory processes in healthy individuals
summary:
Chronic inflammation can lead to various diseases over the course of a person’s life. For example, persistent inflammation can cause rheumatism or intestinal disorders. In neurological conditions such as multiple sclerosis (MS) or chronic kidney disease (CKD), inflammation and the immune system’s response also get out of control. In principle, inflammation in the body is a natural response by the immune system to fend off and eliminate pathogens and harmful substances. However, when these mechanisms occur to a pathological extent, they can further exacerbate existing conditions and cause a wide range of clinical deficits and limitations.
The latest research findings show that the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) plays a central role in these inflammation- and immune-mediated processes across various diseases. The receptor is found in nearly all organs and cells of the human body.
MS is a neurological disease in which nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord are damaged. In animal models, it has been shown that activation of this receptor suppresses the inflammatory processes associated with MS. This protects the nerve cells from further destruction in the long term. Patients with MS also have lower levels of the receptor in their blood.
Activation of the receptor is also important for maintaining the integrity of the intestinal barrier. The intestinal barrier acts as a kind of “barrier” and consists of four distinct layers, each of which acts as a barrier against pathogens or harmful substances: the bacteria in the gut—collectively known as the microbiome—a mucus layer, the intestinal wall cells, and the gut’s immune system. A leaky or unstable intestinal barrier (also known as “leaky gut”) is discussed as a trigger for many conditions, such as irritable bowel syndrome, chronic inflammatory bowel diseases, food intolerances, and even diseases that extend beyond the gut. Insufficient activation of AhR weakens the intestinal barrier, allowing toxic substances to accumulate in the body; these substances are then inadequately excreted, for example, in patients with CKD.
Various molecules—known as ligands—that can influence AhR activity have already been identified. These include ligands with negative properties, such as toxins that must be excreted via the kidneys (urinary toxins). These toxins accumulate when a person consumes particularly large amounts of animal protein. There are also ligands with beneficial effects on the AhR, such as yellow plant pigments (flavones) or phytochemicals
like indole-3-carbinol. In addition, during the digestion of plant-based foods by gut bacteria (the microbiome), breakdown products and intermediates are produced that have beneficial, positive effects on the AhR. Based on these findings, it can be concluded that a plant-based diet has a positive effect on inflammatory processes and immune responses in the body by influencing the AhR.
It is also known that both dietary tryptophan and microbial metabolites can influence communication between the gut and the brain—specifically, satiety signals. We would also like to examine these parameters.
The first TAhRget study at DLR in 2023 already found that a plant-based, high-fiber diet can influence AhR activity via the gut microbiome. Now, in the TAhRget-trp study in 2026, the pathophysiological mechanisms will be investigated in greater depth—with a particular focus on tryptophan metabolism. This essential amino acid is absorbed through the diet and processed in the gut into various AhR-active metabolites. Which bacteria are involved in this process and which breakdown products ultimately exert immunomodulatory effects depend heavily on the individual’s microbiome and diet.
The goal of this TAhRget-trp study is therefore to investigate how tryptophan metabolism links the factors of diet, microbiome, AhR activation, and the immune system in healthy individuals. Additional studies at Charité in Berlin are investigating the influence of diet in patients with MS and CKD.
conditions: The Effect of Different Diets on Tryptophan-Induced AhR Activation

interventions.name:
Pre/V0: Real-life personal diet
D1-D6: Outpatient real-life Western diet
D7/V1: Outpatient real-life Western diet
D8/V2: DLR clinic visit, low-tryptophan diet, application of 2 doses of 500 mg of L-tryptophan
D9/V3: DLR visit, plant-based diet
D10/V4: outpatient plant-based diet
D11/V5: outpat

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
• Body Mass Index 18.5–29.9 kg/m²
• Regular bowel movements every 1–2 days
• Existing health insurance
• Signed informed consent form at the start of the study
Exclusion criteria:
• Diseases, functional disorders, or other conditions that, in the judgment of the study physician, preclude participation
• Existing autoimmune diseases
• Postoperative periods
• Acute infections
• Malnutrition
• Smokers (must have abstained for at least 6 months)
• Individuals following restrictive diets (such as vegan, vegetarian)
• Known food intolerances or allergies
• Weight change > 2 kg in the month prior to study enrollment
• Use of antibiotics within the last 3 months
• Use of serotonergic medications/substances:
SSRI/SNRI antidepressants, MAO inhibitors, tricyclic antidepressants, lithium, triptans, linezolid, tramadol, St. John’s wort or 5-HTP
• Regular use of probiotics and/or prebiotics or other dietary supplements
• Pregnancy and breastfeeding
• Known abuse of medications, drugs, or alcohol
• Legal incapacity or other circumstances that prevent participants from fully understanding the nature, significance, and implications of this study
• Participation in another clinical trial within the last 3 months or in any other biomedical
study within the last month
